results.name: near_example_yes_rate
results.description: Yes rate for targets within 1-3 of some example but not equal to any example; observed below the null mean means the model over-produces "yes" for numerically adjacent targets (too much interval mass), above means it under-produces similarity-based yes.
results.code:
# name: near_example_yes_rate
# description: Yes rate for targets within 1-3 of some example but not equal to any example; observed below the null mean means the model over-produces "yes" for numerically adjacent targets (too much interval mass), above means it under-produces similarity-based yes.
def _parse(df):
    ex = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").to_numpy(dtype=float)
    t = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy().astype(float)
    r = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    return ex, t, r

def test_statistic(df):
    ex, t, r = _parse(df)
    d = np.nanmin(np.abs(ex - t[:, None]), axis=1)
    m = (d >= 1) & (d <= 3)
    return float(r[m].mean()) if m.any() else 0.0

results.name: parity_mismatch_yes_rate
results.description: Yes rate for targets whose parity differs from that of every example, among sets whose examples all share one parity; observed above the null mean means the model under-produces "yes" for parity-violating targets (too sharp an odd/even rule).
results.code:
# name: parity_mismatch_yes_rate
# description: Yes rate for targets whose parity differs from that of every example, among sets whose examples all share one parity; observed above the null mean means the model under-produces "yes" for parity-violating targets (too sharp an odd/even rule).
def _parse(df):
    ex = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").to_numpy(dtype=float)
    t = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy().astype(float)
    r = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    return ex, t, r

def test_statistic(df):
    ex, t, r = _parse(df)
    par = np.where(np.isnan(ex), np.nan, ex % 2)
    mx = np.nanmax(par, axis=1); mn = np.nanmin(par, axis=1)
    uni = (mx == mn) & ((~np.isnan(ex)).sum(axis=1) >= 2)
    m = uni & ((t % 2) != mn)
    return float(r[m].mean()) if m.any() else 0.0

results.name: parity_match_gap
results.description: Among sets of >=2 examples all of one parity, yes rate for same-parity targets minus yes rate for opposite-parity targets; observed below the null mean means the model exaggerates how much humans generalise along parity.
results.code:
# name: parity_match_gap
# description: Among sets of >=2 examples all of one parity, yes rate for same-parity targets minus yes rate for opposite-parity targets; observed below the null mean means the model exaggerates how much humans generalise along parity.
def _parse(df):
    ex = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").to_numpy(dtype=float)
    t = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy().astype(float)
    r = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    return ex, t, r

def test_statistic(df):
    ex, t, r = _parse(df)
    par = np.where(np.isnan(ex), np.nan, ex % 2)
    mx = np.nanmax(par, axis=1); mn = np.nanmin(par, axis=1)
    uni = (mx == mn) & ((~np.isnan(ex)).sum(axis=1) >= 2)
    same = uni & ((t % 2) == mn); diff = uni & ((t % 2) != mn)
    if not same.any() or not diff.any():
        return 0.0
    return float(r[same].mean() - r[diff].mean())

results.name: trial_index_slope
results.description: OLS slope of rating on trial_index scaled per 100 trials; a nonzero observed slope far from the null (which should be ~0 since the model has no time dependence) means humans' yes rate drifts over the session in a way the model cannot produce.

results.name: out_of_range_minus_in_range
results.description: Yes rate for targets outside [min, max] of the examples minus yes rate for targets inside that range (sets with >=2 examples); observed above the null mean means the model over-weights interval/magnitude generalisation relative to humans (or under-generalises beyond the range).
results.code:
# name: out_of_range_minus_in_range
# description: Yes rate for targets outside [min, max] of the examples minus yes rate for targets inside that range (sets with >=2 examples); observed above the null mean means the model over-weights interval/magnitude generalisation relative to humans (or under-generalises beyond the range).
def _parse(df):
    ex = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").to_numpy(dtype=float)
    t = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy().astype(float)
    r = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    return ex, t, r

def test_statistic(df):
    ex, t, r = _parse(df)
    lo = np.nanmin(ex, axis=1); hi = np.nanmax(ex, axis=1)
    k = (~np.isnan(ex)).sum(axis=1) >= 2
    inr = k & (t >= lo) & (t <= hi); out = k & ~((t >= lo) & (t <= hi))
    if not inr.any() or not out.any():
        return 0.0
    return float(r[out].mean() - r[inr].mean())

results.name: set_size_yes_gap
results.description: Yes rate on 1-2-example sets minus yes rate on 4-example sets (excluding targets that are examples); observed below the null mean means the model's size principle shrinks generalisation with more examples more strongly than humans do (and above means less strongly).
results.code:
# name: set_size_yes_gap
# description: Yes rate on 1-2-example sets minus yes rate on 4-example sets (excluding targets that are examples); observed below the null mean means the model's size principle shrinks generalisation with more examples more strongly than humans do (and above means less strongly).
def _parse(df):
    ex = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").to_numpy(dtype=float)
    t = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy().astype(float)
    r = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    return ex, t, r

def test_statistic(df):
    ex, t, r = _parse(df)
    n = (~np.isnan(ex)).sum(axis=1)
    notin = ~(ex == t[:, None]).any(axis=1)
    a = notin & (n <= 2); b = notin & (n == 4)
    if not a.any() or not b.any():
        return 0.0
    return float(r[a].mean() - r[b].mean())

results.name: target_in_set_yes_rate
results.description: Yes rate on trials whose target is itself one of the shown examples; observed below the model's null mean means the model over-predicts "yes" for already-seen examples (humans say no to them far more than a near-certain concept-membership model allows).
results.code:
# name: target_in_set_yes_rate
# description: Yes rate on trials whose target is itself one of the shown examples; observed below the model's null mean means the model over-predicts "yes" for already-seen examples (humans say no to them far more than a near-certain concept-membership model allows).
def _parse(df):
    ex = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").to_numpy(dtype=float)
    t = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy().astype(float)
    r = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    return ex, t, r

def test_statistic(df):
    ex, t, r = _parse(df)
    m = (ex == t[:, None]).any(axis=1)
    return float(r[m].mean()) if m.any() else 0.0
